title: Bivouac
summary: A minimalist overnight stop with a bivy sack, a tarp or no shelter at all. The traditional choice of fast-and-light alpinists who prefer to carry less and move more.
tips: Choose a site protected from wind and out of the path of rockfall or spindrift.
Insulate from below: a foam pad and your rope or pack under your legs is worth as much as a sleeping bag.
Eat and drink before settling in; the body generates heat by digesting food.
Keep boots, gas and water bottle inside your bag to prevent freezing.

title: Mountain Tents
summary: Four-season tents with strong poles, low profiles and snow valances withstand storms at altitude. The workhorse of every expedition from Denali to Everest.
tips: Pitch with the door leeward and the narrowest end into the wind.
Build snow walls and use deadman anchors; stakes alone do not hold in soft snow.
Ventilate: condensation soaks sleeping bags and can freeze overnight.
Never cook in a closed tent. Carbon monoxide kills silently, so keep a vent open at all times.

title: Snow Caves
summary: Dug into a deep, consolidated drift, a snow cave is silent, windproof and holds a steady temperature around 0 °C regardless of the storm outside.
tips: Dig the entrance below the sleeping platform so warm air is trapped; the sleeping shelf should be higher than the door.
Poke a ventilation hole in the roof and keep it open; mark the outside with an ice axe.
Keep the ceiling domed so meltwater runs down the walls instead of dripping.
Wear waterproofs while digging to stay dry, and keep your shovel inside with you at night.

title: Igloos
summary: Built from blocks of wind-packed snow, an igloo is a structural masterpiece that can sleep a team in comfort where no deep drift exists to dig into.
tips: Cut blocks from firm, uniform wind slab with a snow saw; the quarry becomes the floor.
Spiral the blocks inwards in a continuous ramp, bevelling each so they lean on their neighbours.
Seal gaps with loose snow; the walls will sinter and strengthen as they cure.
Build the entrance tunnel lower than the sleeping platform to create a cold sink.

title: Tarp & Bivy
summary: The lightest realistic shelter. Under a taut tarp on a trekking pole, or simply wrapped in a bivy, it keeps off the wind and most of the precipitation for very little weight.
tips: Pitch high and pitch tight: a taut tarp sheds rain where a slack one gathers weight and collapses.
Choose a sheltered spot below an obvious rock or ice feature; never pitch under a cornice.
Keep the windward side low and the leeward side slightly open for ventilation.
A bright inner layer bounces your body heat back and cuts the wind chill dramatically.

title: Snow Wells & Trenches
summary: When there is no deep drift to dig a cave into, you dig down instead. A snow well or trench uses the insulative snow layer below the surface.
tips: Dig where the snow is deep and wind-free: a trench on the lee side of a mound is ideal.
Make the walls high and the roof domed; cut an entrance lower than the sleeping platform.
Pile the excavated snow on the roof as insulation, but keep the ceiling domed so meltwater runs off.
Label the entrance with an ice axe or a bamboo wand so nobody in the team walks in by mistake.

title: Mountain Huts
summary: From the Refuge du Goûter to the Hörnlihütte, staffed or unstaffed huts provide warm meals, dry beds and a base for summit days. They are the backbone of European alpine culture.
tips: Book well ahead; popular huts on Mont Blanc and the Matterhorn fill months in advance.
Carry a hut sleeping liner, earplugs and a headtorch; lights go out early and alarms ring before dawn.
Respect hut etiquette: boots off at the door, quiet after 21:00, tidy gear away.
Check the opening season and weather conditions; winter rooms are often basic and unheated.
